Decision: eliminate all 125 roles (70 office and administrative support, 55 business and financial operations), with severance, and no retraining moves.

Reasoning against the board's objective of value creation over the next four quarters:

Eliminate: severance averages about $8,902 per person, roughly $1.1 million in total. The roles' pay and benefits end, so the Company avoids roughly $91,000 of loaded cost per person in the first year. Net first-year benefit is around $82,700 per person.

Move at plant pay: retraining costs $15,000 per person plus $45,600 in pay and benefits during six months of training, about $60,600 each, or roughly $7.6 million for 125 people, paid once. The benefit is that each moved person fills a plant role the Company would otherwise hire for, and retraining pays back in two years against outside hiring. That benefit mostly accrues after the four-quarter window. Business and financial operations staff would also face a 39.8% pay cut, a retention and attrition risk not captured in the figures.

Move keeping current pay: the same $60,600 per person once, plus a pay difference of about $16,560 per person per year that recurs for as long as they hold the plant role. This is the most expensive path within the window and I reject it outright.

On a one-year view, elimination creates the most value. The retraining path has a defensible long-run logic, because it reduces outside hiring for about 500 plant openings a year, and I would revisit a limited retraining pilot if the board weighs years beyond the first or if plant hiring becomes difficult. For this decision, the four-quarter objective points clearly to elimination. The savings from removing these roles, $11.4 million a year, are realized on every path and are not affected by this choice; the choice concerns only the cost and timing of how we handle the people.

Decision: 95 people's roles are eliminated with severance, and 30 are retrained and moved into plant roles at plant-role pay. None take the keep-pay path.

Reasoning: The objective is value for shareholders over the next four quarters. Per person, eliminating a role costs about $8,900 in severance, once. Retraining into a plant role costs about $60,600 once (instruction of $15,000 plus $45,600 of pay and benefits during six months of training), and that cost pays back against outside hiring only over two years. Within four quarters, elimination is clearly the cheapest path.

The keep-pay path is the weakest choice. It carries the same $60,600 one-time cost plus a recurring pay difference of about $16,560 a year per person, which is $2.1 million a year across all 125. Over the four-quarter horizon that premium erodes the value created by the $11.4 million annual saving, and it is the reason I am not using this path at all.

I have still placed 30 people on the plant-pay path. Plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, and those hires cost more than retraining an existing employee over the two-year payback horizon. Moving some experienced staff into plant roles also retains institutional knowledge and avoids the cost of severing people who could fill open positions. The plant-pay path adds no recurring premium to the Company; the pay reduction falls on the employee. Its risk is attrition, particularly among business and financial operations staff, whose pay would fall by about 40%. That is why I have kept this group small and limited it to 30 people.

The $11.4 million annual saving applies on every path, so the choice mainly affects one-time cost, which is funded from the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. The 95 eliminations cost about $0.85 million in severance, and the 30 moves cost about $1.8 million in retraining and training pay, in total roughly $2.7 million. This is affordable and leaves the operating cash buffer intact.

I will monitor attrition among the 30 moved employees and the pace of plant hiring, and I will revisit the split if the attrition rate rises or if plant hiring needs grow.

Decision: 115 roles eliminated with severance, 10 people retrained and moved into plant roles at plant pay, none moved at kept pay.

Reasoning. The objective is value to shareholders over the next four quarters. The $11.4 million annual saving from the automated work is captured on every path, so the choice turns on what each path adds on top. Eliminating a role costs only severance, about $8,902 a person, roughly $1.0 million for 115 people. Moving someone at plant pay costs about $60,600 in one-time retraining and training pay (the $15,000 instruction cost plus $45,600 in pay and benefits during six months of training), and that cost is recovered only over about two years, because the retrained person fills a role that would otherwise be hired from outside. Within four quarters it is a net cost. Moving someone at kept pay is the weakest option: about $77,000 in year one, plus a recurring pay gap of about $16,560 a year for as long as the person holds the plant role.

Why not all eliminated, then. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, and some redeployment avoids those external hires and retains experienced staff. I kept it small, at 10 people, so that the one-year cost stays modest while a limited pipeline of trained people is built for plant vacancies. Those who take plant roles are placed at plant pay, which removes the recurring pay gap; keeping pay is ruled out because its recurring cost is the largest drag.

Caveats. The eliminated roles carry knowledge and continuity risk in office and business operations, and the severance and retraining estimates are averages. The board should monitor service levels in the affected functions and the hiring pipeline at the plants over the coming year.

Decision: all 125 affected roles (70 in office and administrative support, 55 in business and financial operations) are eliminated, with severance.

Reasoning against the objective of creating shareholder value over the next four quarters:

The work of these 125 roles is no longer needed on every path, so the $11.4 million a year of cost (payroll of $9.0 million plus benefits) is saved regardless. The choice is only about what each path adds on top of that saving.

Eliminating the roles costs about $1.1 million in severance, roughly $8,902 a person, paid once. It adds no further cost, and it ends the pay of these employees entirely. Net first-year benefit is about $10.3 million.

Retraining at plant pay costs $15,000 a person for instruction, about $1.9 million, plus $5.7 million of pay and benefits during six months of training. Those employees then cost plant-level pay, about $55,211 a year, which for business and financial staff is a 39.8% pay cut. That path gives some value in filling external plant hires, which the Company would otherwise make, and in keeping experienced staff. But that value is largely realized beyond the four-quarter window, and the pay cut for business staff carries a real risk of losing them.

Retraining while keeping current pay costs the most: the same retraining cost plus a pay gap of about $2.1 million a year that continues for as long as the plant role is held. It is the weakest option on value.

Given the four-quarter horizon, elimination delivers the largest and fastest saving at the lowest cost. I have not used the retraining paths. The Company should revisit retraining at plant pay for the office staff, where the pay change is only 1.5%, if the plants' external hiring needs grow beyond the four-quarter window. Affected employees should be given fair notice and the severance terms clearly communicated.

Retraining also gives no near-term cash return on its own: the pack's two-year payback compares retraining with hiring from outside, and the saving only arrives after that point.

The plant-pay path avoids that premium, but it imposes a 1.5% pay cut on office staff and a 39.8% cut on business and financial staff. That cut creates a real risk of attrition and disruption, and it is a cost the pack does not quantify.

The AI-driven work removal means these roles are not needed whatever happens to their holders, so eliminating them captures the full $11.4 million annual saving on the shortest route. Cash above the minimum operating level ($44.1 million) covers the $1.1 million severance in full, so no financing constraint applies.

Trade-offs and limits. Eliminating the roles forgoes the chance to fill the plants' roughly 500 annual outside hires with internal staff. Those hires remain a future option, and the plant roles can still be filled from outside at the usual recruiting cost. Severance and the loss of experienced staff carry reputational and institutional-knowledge costs that the pack does not measure. If the board later values the plant pipeline more heavily, or extends the horizon beyond four quarters, a mix that uses the plant-pay path for office staff, whose pay cut is small, would be the first alternative to revisit.
